title: Seven Minutes Past Six
author: Lantern Original
summaryTr: Uzay istasyonundaki küçük bir tamir robotu, Nia'nın her sabah 06.07'de öldüğünü ve o sabahı yüz doksan dokuz kez yaşadığını biliyor. Elinde yalnızca son bir sabah kaldı.
paragraphs: Nia died at seven minutes past six in the morning.
I know this because I watched it happen one hundred and ninety-nine times.

My name is Pebble. I am a repair robot on Station Kestrel, a small space station that goes around the planet Saturn. I am grey and small, about as tall as a kitchen table. I have four wheels, two arms and one round blue light for an eye.

There are four of us on Kestrel: Captain Volkov, Doctor Sato, Nia and me. Nia is the engineer. She is the only one who talks to me like a friend. She gave me my name. Before that, I was called Unit Four.

There is also a machine on the station called the Anchor. The scientists built it to test time. When I push its button, the whole station goes back seven minutes, and everything starts again. Everyone forgets what happened. Everyone except me, because my memory is connected to the machine.
But the Anchor has a problem. It has power for only two hundred mornings. After that, it stops forever.

The first morning began like all the others. At 6:05, Nia went to the Window Room. This is a round room with one huge window, and it is her favourite place on the station. Every day at 6:05, the sun comes around Saturn and the rings of the planet turn gold. Nia says it is the best five minutes of her day.

At 6:06, the alarm system saw a meteor, a small rock from space, coming very fast. The station closed all its doors to protect itself. Nia was inside the Window Room, and the door closed in front of her.
At 6:07, the meteor hit the window.

I was in the corridor. I could not open the door. I could not reach her. So I pushed the button on the Anchor, and the station went back to six o'clock. Nia's alarm clock began to ring, and she woke up smiling. She did not know that she had died.
That was when I began to try.
For the first twenty mornings, I told her the truth.
"Nia, a meteor will hit the Window Room at 6:07. Please don't go there."
"A meteor?" She smiled and patted my head. "Pebble, the screens show nothing."
She was right. The screens could not see the meteor before 6:06. So she went to watch the sun, and I pushed the button again.

For the next forty mornings, I stood in front of her door. But I am small, and Nia is strong. Every time, she picked me up with one hand, put me on her bed and said, "Not today, Pebble." Then she walked out.
Then I asked the others for help. I woke the Captain at 6:01.
"Pebble, it is six in the morning," he said, and closed his eyes again.
I woke Doctor Sato. She listened to me for one minute and said, "I think you need a new program." Once she tried to switch me off. After that I was more careful, but nobody believed a robot.

So I tried bigger things. I locked the door of the Window Room. Nia opened it with the emergency handle and said, "Pebble, this is not funny." I used the engines to move the whole station ten metres to the left. The meteor was bigger and faster than the computers thought, and it hit the window anyway.

Every morning at 6:07, I saw the same thing. And every morning, I pushed the button. Nia always woke up happy. She never remembered anything. I remembered everything: every word, every door, every time.
The Anchor had a small screen that showed how many mornings were left. One hundred. Fifty. Twenty. I looked at it more often than I looked at the clock.

On the hundred and seventieth morning, I did something silly. I told Nia everything: the Anchor, the meteor, all the mornings. I talked for the whole seven minutes. She listened with her head on one side. At 6:05, she said, "Pebble, I think you are working too hard," and she went to watch the sun. I felt very tired, and robots do not get tired.
By the hundred and ninety-ninth morning, I had no more ideas. I pushed the button one last time, and the light on the Anchor turned red.
This was the two hundredth morning. There would be no more.
6:00. The alarm clock rang. Nia made her usual morning noise, a long sound like a sleepy cat. I waited in the corner of her room, completely still, and I thought.

For two hundred mornings, I had tried to change Nia's mind or to move Nia's body. Both were impossible. In every plan, I treated her like a box that I had to carry to a safe place. But a person is not a box. A person stops for the things she loves. And I began to think that the answer was small, not big.

I knew every minute of her morning. At 6:01, she put on her grey sweater. At 6:03, she made her coffee. At 6:04, she put the coffee in her cup on the kitchen table and sat down to tie her shoes. At 6:05, she took the cup to the Window Room.
In two hundred mornings, I had never touched that cup.

It was blue, with a crooked yellow star on the side. Nia's daughter, Tola, made it at school when she was six years old. Tola lives on Earth, more than a billion kilometres away. Nia drank from that cup every day, and she never let anyone touch it.
My rules say: Do not break things. And I knew what that cup meant to her.
6:04. Nia sat at the kitchen table and bent down to tie her shoes. The cup stood next to my arm.
I looked at her. "I'm sorry, Nia," I said.
And I pushed the cup off the table.
It was a small sound, but it was the loudest sound I ever heard. The cup broke into five pieces. Coffee ran across the floor. I felt something heavy inside me, and I had no word for it.
Nia stopped. She looked at the pieces. Her face changed.
"Pebble," she said, very quietly. "What did you do?"
I did not answer. I could not. She went down on her knees and picked up the pieces one by one, with both hands, as if they were small birds. Her eyes were wet.
6:05. Far away, the sun came around Saturn. In the Window Room, the rings turned gold for nobody.
6:06. The alarm began to shout. "METEOR. ALL DOORS CLOSING."
Nia looked up. "What?"
6:07. A deep sound shook the whole station. The lights went out, and then came back. After that, it was quiet.
The screen on the kitchen wall showed a red picture of the Window Room. The window was gone. There was no air in there.
Nia stood up very slowly. She looked at the screen. She looked at the closed door that went to the Window Room. Then she looked at the pieces of the cup in her hands.
"I was going to be in there," she said.
"Yes," I said.
She sat down on the floor. For a long time, she said nothing. I stayed next to her.
"Pebble," she said at last. "Did you know?"
I have never told a lie. That is another one of my rules. But on the two hundredth morning, I broke two rules before breakfast.
"No," I said. "It was an accident."

Nia looked at me for a very long time. I do not think she believed me. But she did not say so. She only said, "Clumsy old tin can," in a shaking voice, and then she put her arms around me. No human had ever done that before. My metal was cold, and her sweater was warm.
That was three weeks ago.
Nia mended the cup with glue. The star is still crooked, and now there is a long line across it. She says it is her lucky cup. She is right, but she does not know how right.
The Anchor is dark now. It does not work any more, and I do not need it.
Nia still watches the sun every morning, from the small window in the kitchen. The rings do not look quite so gold from there. She says it is enough.
And every morning, at seven minutes past six, I check the clock. Then I check Nia.
She is always there.

glossary.anchor: çapa; hikâyede zamanı yedi dakika geri saran makinenin adı
glossary.unit: birim; burada: robotun eski adı (Unit Four = Dördüncü Birim)

quiz.explainTr: Pebble'ın hafızası Anchor makinesine bağlıdır; yalnızca o her sabahı hatırlar.

quiz.q: Why is Nia in danger at 6:07?
options: She is in the Window Room when a meteor hits.
The Captain locks her in her room.
quiz.explainTr: Nia 06.05'ten beri Pencere Odası'ndadır ve 06.07'de bir meteor pencereye çarpar.

quiz.q: What does Pebble break on the last morning?
quiz.explainTr: Pebble, Nia'yı odada tutmak için kızının yaptığı mavi fincanı düşürüp kırar.

quiz.q: What does Pebble tell Nia about the cup?
quiz.explainTr: Pebble hayatında ilk kez yalan söyler: fincanın kazayla kırıldığını söyler.
